sections.overview: Dipylidium caninum is a common tapeworm of dogs and cats and only occasionally infects people; it is also called the flea or cucumber tapeworm.
sections.identification: The adult is a segmented cestode; gravid segments can pass in stool or emerge near the anus, and each segment can release packets of eggs.
sections.habitat: The adult tapeworm lives in the small intestine of its dog or cat definitive host, while immature stages develop in fleas or, less often, chewing lice.
sections.diet: The cited veterinary accounts describe an intestinal parasite attached to the host’s gut lining, but do not give a species-specific account of nutrient uptake.
sections.behavior: Dogs and cats usually acquire infection by swallowing an infected adult flea while grooming; people can become infected accidentally by swallowing an infected flea or louse.
sections.reproduction: Egg packets released from gravid segments are eaten by flea or louse larvae, where the parasite develops to an infective cysticercoid before that insect reaches adulthood.
sections.ecology: Its life cycle links a mammal host with flea or louse intermediate hosts, so controlling ectoparasites is central to breaking transmission between pets.
sections.conservation: This parasite is managed as a veterinary and occasional zoonotic infection, not through a wildlife conservation assessment; prevention centers on flea control and veterinary treatment.
